speechtext:
On the orders of the day yesterday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) requested an explanation regarding the sittings of the committee on privileges and elections. I did not at the time gather the full purport of the question and I asked to be allowed to give the hon. gentleman an answer last night at eight o'clock. Inasmuch as the house was in committee of the whole on resumption at eight o'clock I had no opportunity of making a statement on the matter, and I should like to do So now. I have read Hansard carefully and I find that the leader of the opposition stated that according to the votes and proceedings on May 3 the committee on privileges and elections had been called for Tuesday, May 8 -that is, to-day-while, according to the votes and proceedings of the next day, May 4, the committee is now scheduled to meet on May 10 instead. The hon. member asks for an explanation, and he follows this up with the statement that he had already made arrangements to be present on May 8, this change in dates being of course inconvenient to him. I may offer this explanation. The last day on which the committee met was Thursday, May 3, and when the committee rose, to resume at the call of the chair, I immediately went to the clerk and asked him to reserve, as the date of the next meeting, May 8. This was suggested tentatively because I was not sure at the time whether certain documents which are expected from the Attorney General of the province of Alberta would be available on that date. Nevertheless, seeing that we have experienced considerable difficulty and a good deal of trouble in getting together not only this but other committees, and as there are not sufficient rooms available for the committees, I deemed it wise to retain May 8 as the next date of meeting. I thought it best to reserve that date at once and I asked the clerk to arrange accordingly. I was not then aware that the mere fact of my asking the clerk to reserve May 8 would mean the printing of that date in the votes and proceedings as

Athabaska Election
the next date of meeting. Unfortunately this was done, and the following day, May 4, being afraid that the documents for which we were waiting would not be available on May 8, and not wishing to have the committee meet unnecessarily, I went back to the clerk and requested him to make it May 10 instead of May 8. There might be a further explanation regarding the necessity for the documents to which I have referred, but I do not think that my hon. friend's question bears any relation to that. As regards the inconvenience caused the hon. gentleman, I express my regret. It is my mistake and I am sorry.

Pension Act

I would suggest that
the minister explain the nature of the proposed legislation.

As the house
knows, when pension matters were under discussion last session it was understood that during this session a special committee would be appointed to include members of all groups in this house, Which would make an inquiry into certain matters which had been brought to the attention of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment by various soldier and other organizations throughout the country dealing with pension legislation. DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Department of National Revenue Act be amended to provide that the minister be empowered to appoint certain classes of officers with sueh salaries or remuneration as may be determined by the governor in council, and that a gratuity may be paid any officer on retirement in lieu of a period of leave of absence with pay, with further provisions as to filling vacancies by transfers and promotions for the betterment of the service.
Hon. R.	B. BENNETT (Leader of	the
Opposition):	Mr. Speaker, before this
resolution goes to	the committee	stage, Idesire to say that we who sit on your left are strongly and unrelentingly opposed to the principle of the resolution in its present form. It	means	the recurrence	of	thepatronage	system,	which should	not	be
tolerated in this country. It is not conducive to good service, or to the public weal. While there have been many defects in connection with the administration of the civil service, the fact is that it is a great advance over anything we have heretofore had in this country. We protest against any effort being made to return to the old condition of patronage.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps I might make a
statement with regard to the resolution as it stands. The resolution, as well as the bill, which is based upon the resolution, is in accord with certain recommendations made by the royal commission investigating the Customs department. Perhaps I should offer an apology for the resolution being in the form in which it is at present, and I would like to remove some misconceptions that apparently have arisen from the text of the resolution itself.
The bill, which is founded upon the resolution, does not go nearly as far as the resolution does. The resolution itself calls for power to be given to the minister to make certain appointments. As a matter of fact, the bill does not give to the minister power to make any appointments whatsoever, although the commission recommended that such power be given to the minister. I may say, for the information of the committee, that whereas it was intended that such power should be given to the minister, I do not
care myself to go that distance, because I do not feel inclined to interfere any further than seems to me to be necessary with the work of the Civil Service Commission.
I would state what actually appears in the bill. The bill is printed; I am not sure whether it is on the file, but it is ready for consideration. Briefly, it does this: It asks that appraisers, who are technical officers in the Department of Excise, preventive officers, and special investigating officers be nominated bj' the minister. That is, the selection to be made by the minister, or by officers under his control, or by a committee, or, in the case of the appraisers, by the Dominion board of appraisers. The minister will make the nominations to the Civil Service Commission and the Civil Service Commission will make the appointments within a specified time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How many
officers would that affect?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should think about 125
out of a list of, say, 5,500 in the department. Only a small section of the employees are affected by the bill.
The minister makes the nomination, as stated, to the Civil Service Commission and the commission will make the appointment within fifteen days. That time may not be considered long enough, or possibly a shorter period may be sufficient. On the failure of the commission to make the appointment, it may then be made, on the recommendation of the minister, by governor in council. I draw the attention of the committee to this fact, that the minister himself has not the power to make the appointment, More than that, he has removed from his jurisdiction, to some extent at least, appointments in the preventive service which he now has power to make. He makes the recommendation to the commission, and if the commission does not make the appointment, as recommended, it may then be made by governor in council.
The bill further provides, and this is also in accord with the recommendation of the royal commission, that transfers of collectors and surveyors may be made from one port to another. Instances occur in which a collector may not be well fitted for the particular position he holds, and there may be a collector in a smaller port who has proven his special fitness for the higher position. In this way, it will be possible for the department to place men in the positions for which they are best qualified.
There is one other provision, which I do not think will cause any opposition, at least
National Revenue Act

I hope it will not. It applies to cases where a vacancy occurs by reason of the retirement of an official. Instead of the position remaining vacant for six months, as is now the case, the position may be declared vacant at once, and be immediately filled. As we have it now, when an official retires he is given six months' retiring allowance; six months' leave of absence, as it were. The position is not actually vacant, although the man has left his post and receives his pay for six months. We would still give him his retiring allowance of six months, but the position becomes vacant immediately, and the new appointment could be made at once. In that way, there would be no interference with the work of the department.
Mr. Chairman, that is practically all that is in the bill. I would like to point out that there is, to my mind, practically no interference whatever with the principle of the Civil Service Act. I personally desire to avoid that as much as possible and I am quite sincere in that, although I see my hon. friend opposite is giving himself over to merriment. I do not like the practice which would no doubt grow up of the minister being importuned from all sides to make appointments, and I desire to avoid that. The proposal is made with the intention of promoting the efficiency of the Department of National Revenue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the object of going through the pretence or farce of saying that the Civil Service Commission makes appointments, when the minister very distinctly says, I make the recommendation and if you do not appoint the man I recommend, I will appoint him myself?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In the first place I agree
with the royal commission which felt that in the case of officers such as apraisers where special skill and qualifications are required, the department is in a better position than the Civil Service Commission to make the selection of those skilled officers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What then is the use of bringing in the Civil Service Commission unless it be as a sort of camouflage ?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In the first instance I was
disposed to accept the recommendation of the committee just as it stood, but certain representations were made to me-and I saw the force of them-that it might be possible and perhaps would be the case that under such conditions the minister might not make such appointments as he ought to make; in other 
words, to be perfectly frank, that political pressure might be brought to bear upon him and he might appoint men to positions as appraisers on the score more of politics than of efficiency. It was felt-and I think there is something in the contention-that if in every instance the minister were obliged to make those recommendations to the Civil Service Commission, he would not be nearly so prone to go to the commission with improper recommendations, have his recommendations turned down again and again as they might be, and have the people learn the reason why they were so turned down. This is intended only to operate as a brake upon the minister exercising the power in an improper manner. There is the further brake upon the minister that if the commission fails to make the appointment, he does not then himself make it, but his recommendations and nominations must pass the scrutiny of the governor in council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under this legislation what
becomes of the preference now provided for the returned men?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would think that the same consideration would be exercised in all cases although perhaps I should qualify that in this way. There will be one primary purpose in the mind of the department in making appointments of appraisers or special investigating officers. While every consideration should be given to the returned men and to the appraisers already in the service, other things being equal, in the cause of efficiency in the department, because the appraisers are perhaps the most important officers you can have in the Customs department, I would not hesitate, if it were necessary, to go outside in order to get the best man for the job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is all very well. The
Civil Service Commission is to make the appointment and I take it that the commission will be compelled to act within a prescribed jurisdiction in that it must give the preference to the returned man. Does the minister propose that where such a preference has been given, it may be over-ridden by the minister himself or by the governor in council

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not sure that I can say anything more than I have already said. The department will select the man best fitted in their opinion for the position. If the commission for any reason-and it might be for the reason suggested by my hon. friend- declines to make the appointment, then it will be within the purview of the governor in council to make it. The criticism may be raised that in some instances the returned

National Revenue Act
soldier might not receive the position, but I believe it would surely be, as I think it ought to be, the will of the house that the very first purpose to be served, especially in connection with a department which has been so much criticized, is to obtain the most efficient men to carry on the work. That is the one thought that has been in my mind in the preparation of the bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the
minister or the Civil Service Commission determine whether or not the returned soldier or any other person has the necessary qualifications?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In the case of appraisers the
recommendation coming from the department, from the minister, although the minister will personally not make the selection, will be made through the board of appraisers. They will make the selection in the first instance, as I have stated, on the primary factor of efficiency. That will stand; I can see no recession from that. Other things being equal, the returned man and also the men who are already in the service of the department should receive the preference. I should like to disabuse the mind of any civil servants, appraisers and others, who feel that they may be sidetracked. There is no such intention. I propose to promote the men in my department if they are efficient, but as I said before- and I hope the committee will bear me out in this-I would not hesitate to make a recommendation and to ask for the appointment of a man even though he came from outside the service, even though he might conceivably not be a returned man, if he were specially and peculiarly fitted for the work which he has to do.
The work which the appraisers have to do is extremely important. The whole efficiency and almost the proper conduct of the Department of Customs depends upon the efficiency of the appraisers. If your appraisal system is wrong, you will certainly not obtain the revenue you ought to obtain. The appraisal system has been criticized very severely by all those bodies that have been investigating the Customs department. Those things which they criticze we want to correct and this is the way in which we desire to correct them. There are those who will say that the Civil Service Commission can make the selections just as well as we can. My opinion is that the Dominion appraisers whom we have selected-the board is not complete, but we have made a beginning-are best qualified to make the selections. Without casting any reflection upon the Civil Service Commission I think we know the men in our department better than the commision can. Therefore I
think that is a fair way to make the appointments and it does not place in the hands of the minister the absolute power to make them. I do not know whether this is the time to read from the report of the royal commission, _ or from the report of the Commercial Protective Association, but if I did they would bear us out in that they recommend our going further than I propose to go under the bill. I have been as moderate as possible, because I do not desire to interfere with the principle of appointments by the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In the case of a man being wanted for a given position, is there in the proposed legislation anything that will oblige the minister to submit more than one name?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What sort of an examination would the Civil Service Commission give to the man recommended to the commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission could make any investigation they desired. That would be entirely within their own province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the Civil Service Commission prescribe an examination or will they not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The examination to decide
what recommendation ought to be made will be made by our own officials, by the board. If the Civil Service Commission wishes to submit the applicant to an examination, that will be absolutely within their power. Following that they can then either make the appointment or reject the nomination.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
After the minister and his
department had recommended a man for a particular position and had given him any examination they might prescribe, the minister would not expect the Civil Service Commission to refuse to make the appointment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I hope not, because I rather
expect the commission would be willing to co-operate with the Department of National Revenue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then why bring the Civil
Service Commission in at all? Does it not seem a perfect blind to mention the Civil Service Commission?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
For the very reason I gave before. It should not, I would say personally, be necessary, but the intention is to put a brake, if you like, on any minister who might abuse the power that would otherwise be given to him. If the Civil Service Commission thinks it is not sufficient, I would be willing to cut that out.
National Revenue Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are two matters
to be dealt with. The minister has dealt with the one, but not with the other. The first relates to the selection of the individual; the second relates to the salary or compensation he is to be paid. With respect to the first, the minister should not endeavour to throw this smoke screen before the public. The civil servants of this country are very greatly concerned about this matter, and merely because, I suppose, I am in the position I am, I receive telegrams and letters from civil servants from Vancouver to Nova Scotia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: So do I.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Doubtless the minister
has received them. The press of the country has referred to the matter in terms, we will say, of delicate criticism, most of them not believing that it would be possible for the minister to revert to the old system of things.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is not possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Let us see what it means in essence. We must not deal with the present incumbent of the office, but we must deal with the office. It is a mistake to assume that because the Hon. William Euler is Minister of National Revenue, there will always be a William Euler in that office, or that he is a particular person that must be selected for some peculiar kind of treatment from this house. An efficient and effective minister we will say he is, for the . sake of argument-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We will assume that for the sake of the argument, although I think before this house rises we will perhaps have to revise our assumption. Let us go a step further. We are now dealing with the office, not the individual, and the office proposes to make a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission for the appointment of given individuals to given posts. That is what is proposed. In other words, whatever pressure may be brought to bear upon the Minister of National Revenue, whoever he may be, that pressure, political,- friendly, family, and every other kind in the world, may succeed in 'inducing the minister, not this minister per-adventure, but a minister, to recommend to the commission the appointment of a particular person. You cannot get away from that. Then why ask the Civil Service Commission to be thus dragged in the mire by making it appear that they are going to appoint somebody that they have no power to 
appoint? They have to appoint the man the minister recommends or nobody at all. Then why drag the Civil Service Commission in? It is nothing but a smoke screen to make the people of this country believe that you are still retaining the Civil Service Commission in all its integrity, while as a matter of fact you are flaunting it and holding it up to scorn before the public. You simply write to the Civil Service Commission. "Dear Sirs:	Enclosed please find the name of the
gentleman we desire to have appointed as appraiser." The days go by and the Civil Service Commission find that he is not the man for the job, and they do not make the appointment. Then the minister goes to the governor in council and makes the appointment.
I come to the next point, the question of salary. As the matter now stands, the civil servants have graded salaries, and there is nothing they are more jealous about than their rights with respect to their salaries. This resolution proposes to appoint persons who will be appraisers not appointed by the Civil Service Commission, and receiving salaries in the discretion of the governor in council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
May I correct my hon.
friend?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The resolution says
"such salaries or remuneration as may be determined by the governor in council."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Exactly, that is what the
resolution says, but I have apologised already for the resolution. The bill does not carry out that idea. It reads:
The officer so appointed by the commission or by the governor in council, as the case may be, shall be paid such salary or remuneration in accordance with the civil service regulations as may be determined by the commission or the governor in council respectively.
My hon. friend will, note that it says, "in accordance with the civil service regulations."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That meets the difficulties I was pointing out to the minister. In other words, instead of the governor in council fixing the salaries, they are to be fixed by the Civil Service Commission. The resolution, of course, says just the opposite. Perhaps the better way for us to proceed would be to have the resolution reported and the bill given its first and second readings, so that with the bill in our hands we may study what the new provisions are as distinguished from the resolution.

*	National Revenue Act

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is exactly the suggestion I desire to make. Perhaps the committee might allow the resolution to be reported, and then the bill can be introduced and read a second time, and the whole matter be discussed in committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Without committing ourselves on this side of the house to any ac-aceptance of principle.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is to prevent the Civil Service Commission having access to the same information which is available to the minister in preparing his recommendations in regard to the qualifications of any individual for the position of appraiser?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The commission cannot possibly have the same knowledge, because they cannot possibly have that knowledge in themselves. speechtext: May I ask whether the minister would advocate the application of this same principle in regard to the appointment of appraisers to other departments of the government?

Our inquiry has shown that the present system of appointing appraisers or other officers requiring expert or technical knowledge is unsatisfactory, and we are convinced that where expert and technical knowledge is required, the examination of the applicants for positions should be conducted by those who are specially qualified to act in the premises.
We are of opinion that all appointments to the office of appraiser at the different ports of the Dominion should be made by the minister after examination of the applicants by tile board of appraisers.
We quite recognize that this method of appointment would conflict with ^ the system now in vogue under the Civil Service Act, but notwithstanding this -we are of opinion that this method should be adopted.

speechtext: Should not the minister take just as seriously the recommendations of the special parliamentary committee that was appointed a couple of years ago to inquire into the Customs department?

That the board (the board of appraisers) be given power to retain such appraisers as they deem competent and qualified, and to appoint with the minister's approval and notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act such further appraisers as may be required from time to time, and to fix subject to the approval of the governor in council the remuneration to be paid to the various grades of appraisers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It looks as if the resolution as it appears on the order paper followed fairly closely the report from which the minister has just quoted. But the difficulty I see is that the minister has announced to the house that the bill which he proposes to introduce does not follow the resolution. The resolution as it appears on the order paper was so approved, but if I gather correctly from the minister's statement, the bill does not follow the resolution in two very important points.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It does not go as far.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In two very important
points of principle the bill involves a serious chance. In the first place, the resolution provides that the minister is to make these

National Revenue Act
appointments; now the minister says that the bill which is based on this resolution empowers the Civil Service Commission to do so. What I am pointing out, Mr. Chairman, is that the bill must follow the resolution. The resolution has been approved by His Excellency the Governor General, and I think the minister is going pretty far in saying that he proposes to introduce a bill very different from the resolution which he is asking the committee to consider. What is the object of passing this resolution if the bill is to be entirely different? Let us have a resolution such as we expect to be incorporated in the bill when it comes forward. If this proceeding is only for the purpose of expediting the matter, I do not know that I would seriously object; but if we are going to pass a resolution in this instance, not to be followed by a bill along the same lines, we can do it in other instances, and there will be no object in the future in introducing resolutions at all. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think the Minister of National Revenue is to be congratulated on his initiative in withdrawing certain classes of officers from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. Whenever the question of appointments by the Civil Service Commission has been discussed in this house it has been pointed out that the most important positions in the service are not under the control of the commission. The minister has good authority for taking this course in the recommendation of the royal commission that investigated the customs. They recommended that certain classes of employees of the Department of National Revenue should not be appointed by the Civil Service Commission, but by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the minister. For my part I should like to see some of the minister's colleagues follow the good example he has set them, as I am fully of the opinion that the ministers and their deputies are much better qualified than the Civil Service Commission to appoint the higher classes of employees. I would rather see the minister take this responsibility himself than leave it to the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the time the Civil Service Commission was appointed I ventured to offer some criticisms as to the wisdom of placing all patronage in the hands of three or four men sitting in Ottawa. At that time I was a voice crying in the wilderness-I was in a hopeless minority. I was treated with the severest censure by those on my own side of the house, and my friends on the Liberal side were unanimous and loud in claiming that all patronage appointments should be taken out of the hands of members of parliament and turned over to the Civil Service Commission, which would be independent of parliament. I expressed the opinion at the

National Revenue Act
time that many appointments, such as postmasters in country districts, should remain in the hands of the member for the constituency, no matter what government was in power.
I contended that so long as the people saw fit to express their confidence by sending him to parliament, he was the man whose recommendation should receive consideration in the making of such appointments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I take no
different position now from what I took then. But there was another reason why I had serious doubts as to the way in which this change would work out. I was very confident that so long as a Conservative government was in power the Grits would force them to hew to the line in leaving all patronage in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. While at that time not one of the oldest members of the house, I had a long experience and extensive knowledge of Grit tactics. I believed then and my belief has since been confirmed absolutely, that once they obtained the reins of office the Civil Service Commission would be practically a dead letter so far as many appointments were concerned. Since this government has been in power the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission have become virtually a dead letter, and we have seen thousands of men arbitrarily appointed through Grit patronage just as in the old days before the Civil Service Commission was brought into being.
Now the commission advertise for applicants for a certain position and they set forth the qualifications required. They report whether the successful applicant posseses the requisite qualifications, and on that recommendation, and under the circumstances, the law distinctly says that the returned soldier, not may, but shall, have the preference. It does not stipulate that he shall possess a university education; if he possesses even the minimum qualifications the law says that he shall have the preference. I do not know to what extent that regulation has been observed by the minister who is interested in this bill, but I do know that I am prepared to prove that one of his colleagues, the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), does not care anything whatever for the laws of the land when it comes to making appointments. I have the facts and I am prepared to show where in a certain instance, out of eight applicants, only one of them was a returned soldier; and although he was not only accepted by the Civil Service Commission as
possessing the necessary qualifications but was appointed to the position, the Postmaster General decided to override the law, to override the report and recommendation of the commission and to appoint one who was not a returned soldier and who did not possess any better qualifications than did the returned man. That is one instance. I will venture to say there are members in this house-[DOT] probably more on this side than on the other, but any number of hon. gentlemen-who could cite cases similar to the one I have mentioned, and which I hope to go into more fully when we are dealing with the Postmaster General's estimates. When that time comes we will fight it out to a finish. I repeat, in view of the experience we have had in the past few years-and every year is getting worse than the year before with this government- for the minister to get up and say the man will be appointed on the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission is the purest kind of farce. It is a bluff, nothing but camouflage. It is hardly worthy of that name, because the minister simply says to the Civil Service Commission: "This is the man you have to appoint, and if you do not appoint him we will take the matter out of your hands and appoint him ourselves. If you do appoint him at our dictation we will say that you are the ones that made the appointment." That is the kind of bunkum put up by the minister to-day and which he wants us to endorse by legislation.
If the government have made up their minds to discard the Civil Service Commission altogether, and to ignore their recommendations, why do they not come out like men and say, " We have tried the thing and in our judgment this procedure is not the proper one; we propose, so far as we are concerned, to discard the Civil Service Commission and make these appointments ourselves." They are doing this anyway without regard for law or anything else. They have been doing it for years and it is getting worse and worse every year. When in opposition hon. gentlemen opposite insisted on hewing to the line, and a minister at that time did not dare suggest such a thing as that he had a better knowledge than the Civil Service Commission as to who should fill a certain office. But as soon as they get the reins of power the Civil Service Act, as well as every other act that interferes with tactics for election purposes, becomes a dead letter. It has been a dead letter ever since this government came into power.

I have read already from
the report of the royal commission, which goes further than the bill, as well as from the report of the Commercial Protective Association, which also goes further than the bill. Someone has raised a point as to the recommendation made by the parliamentary committee of inquiry in 1926, in which no provision is suggested for appointments by the Civil Service Commission. What I have before me states:

The evidence adduced before the committee disclosed two outstanding facts, namely:-First, the methods of appraisal are exceedingly careless and fail to safeguard the interests of the importer, or the revenues of the country from being defrauded by undervaluation; and secondly, persons appointed as appraisers-
And remember, these were appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
-are in many instances untrained in the branch to which they are appointed. The committee recommend that the appraisal branch be reorganized and that all appraisers be chosen because of their competency to estimate the values of the class of goods they are appointed to appraise.
There is nothing said there about appointments by the commission.

It is the law of the
country.

I do not know whether the minister has any further proposals to make; from his observations last night I was inclined to believe that he had. My particular reference is to the question of posting notices in connection with which several suggestions' have been made in committee. Under the proposed amendment the notice will be posted for at least sixty days, and we have suggested that the minister would be well advised to extend that time to at least four months. I would like to call the attention of the committee also to this particular section and to ask the minister the reason for posting the notices as the section is drafted at present. It does not provide for anything, even if you post the notices for sixty days. This seems to me to be quite an innocuous section, and unless it is amended in some form it will have no value at all. You may post a notice for sixty days, but if there is no provision for receiving abjections to the
granting of a certificate, of what value is the posting of the notice? I would like the minister to say if he has any other proposal in mind in reference to these two particulars?

In connection with the question of the proper delay and other matters of that kind I am quite in the hands of the committee. Hon. members from all sides of the house have suggested that perhaps the delay of sixty days would not be long enough, and some have even suggested a delay of six months. I would point out that under the present act there must be a delay of three months; I think it would be going too far to make it any longer, but I am quite willing that we leave the delay as it is in the present act. Therefore I would move that we revert to section 1 of the bill and that the words "ninety days" be substituted for the words "sixty days" in the fifteenth line thereof. I hope this will meet the wishes of the committee.
Amendment agreed to.

I appreciate the manner in which the minister has met our objections, but there is still another point which he has not recognized. If any valuable purpose is to be served by posting a notice for ninety days, some provision must be made for persons residing in the vicinity to file objections to the granting of a certificate. In section 22 as it stands at present no such provision is .made, although in the old act that point was taken care of. I would suggest to the minister that some provision should be made in order that objections to the granting of a certificate of naturalization may be lodged with some person in authority, either with the minister himself or with some person designated by him.

I do not think any additional provision is required on that point, but I am quite willing to declare now that any objections of the kind to which my hon. friend refers always can be brought to the attention of the Secretary of State. In the previous act it was provided that such objections might be presented to the court hearing the applications for naturalization. But now that whole procedure will take place with the department. I do not think it is necessary to have any provision in the bill. I desire to state most positively to my hon. friend that the Department of the Secretary of State will give full consideration to any such provision, as he has just referred to.

Before the bill is
reported I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the language used in
National Revenue Act

the amendment. Opposed as I am to the bill, I have hesitated to address the committee, because I was not in the house yesterday when the matter was so fully discussed. I do not know whether the language used has been discussed or not, but it does seem to me that we are not only using inappropriate language but really stultifying ourselves. "Natural born" can only mean one of two things. A natural bom fool is an idiot from his birth. "Natural bom" either means an idiot, or an illegitimate or natural son. That is a fact. "Natural" means both legitimate and illegitimate, but legitimate only when applied to ordinary affairs and not to birth. "Natural", in connection with birth, has only the one meaning. I think it can then be said that this bill was conceived in iniquity and born in sin. I am unwilling that this house, without an objection from me, should use the words "natural bom" in the sense in which I know the committee intends it, but which is not the true meaning of the words.

I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that the objection is well taken. I might say that that is the very term used in the Australian statute, which has been recommended for imitation by the leader of the opposition himself.

There is another
objection altogether to the term. "Natural born" is the one thing which the minister is not applying to this legislation. Under the bill, Caesar could not get a certificate, or Macbeth could not get one. How will you prove that anyone is "natural bom"? The only people that I think could come under this would be the Indians, who are assured of no medical attention at birth, or the Esquimos or someone like that.

Mr. Chairman,
when we were in committee at the last meeting, clause (b) of section 6 also clause (g) of section 6, and section 14 were allowed to stand in order that they might be further discussed at this meeting. The other sections were adopted.
In regard to clause (b), section 6. My hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) suggested that the word "temporary" should be added after the word "time", in the second line. I think if we will give a little consideration to the section he will find that the addition of the word "temporary" will not improve the section.
What is being sought in this section is to indicate a class which could not possibly be brought under the Civil Service Commission. I will just read the clause:
(b) for the selection and employment of such part time professional officers, or part or full time employees whose compensation is determined by the rates payable for similar work in the locality in which such persons are employed as may be required from time to time for the carrying on of the work with which the minister is charged under this part.
The first class, professional officers, would include consultant surgeons, consultant medical officers, X-ray experts, or some professional class that would not be in the service of the department at all times, but only as required from time to time. We have a class that would be employed part time, such as painters, window cleaners, and men of that type. They would be "part time" and would be paid for the services rendered at the prevailing rates. Then there would be "full time" employees, such as hospital orderlies, cooks, assistant cooks, engineers and firemen. If we will consult the practice in the Department of Public Works, a large employing department, it will be found that there they have a class known as the "prevailing rate class". It is to make provision for these two classes, which do not come within the provisions of the Civil Service Act, that the section is drawn. As I said before, it was drawn' by the Department of Justice, and I think it is quite clear, and would not be improved by adding the word "temporary".

speechtext: I would like to ask the minister regarding a question which was before the committee when this bill was being considered, that is, with reference to certain classes of returned men who were indigent and had no means of providing for medical attention. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This bill gives us power to provide for and take care of that class. The recommendations made by the committee will be given every consideration by the government. The opinion of the committee which made the recommendation along this line was that it should be retroactive; otherwise it would be obviously of no use to the soldier. The intention of the committee was that those men who, they thought, had been unjustly deprived of patents for land by reason of a liability of some other description in respect of a separate transaction with the government, should be relieved and be enabled to secure their homestead without regard to that liability. There is no doubt that the intention was that they should not suffer because of any liability to the government they may have had in the past.

The idea of the committee was that a soldier having received a loan in connection with a quarter-section, that quarter-section should be security for the loan, and that if he had acquired a homestead that homestead should not necessarily be encumbered with the loan which had been granted on the quarter-section. Two soldiers take up two pieces of land; they have a quarter-section each on which they obtained loans; and one takes up a homestead. Now it is manifestly unfair to exact from the one man security in respect of a half-section and from the other man security in respect of a quarter-section. I submit-and this was the intention of the committee-that if a soldier took up a quarter-section on which he obtained a loan and then acquired a homestead, the homestead should not be encumbered but should be left free, unless some specified sum had been advanced on that homestead. I think the words "or otherwise" ought to be deleted. That phrase includes all lands he has acquired, whether by purchase or by way of homestead.

Possibly the hon. member (Mr. Adshead) is under a slight misapprehension. The purpose of the committee was to release the Dominion lands-and by Dominion lands I do not mean lands acquired by purchase but lands still belonging to the Dominion; that is to say, lands on which entry was made, patent to be afterwards issued. We must differentiate between Dominion lands which are purchased and become private pro-
[Mr. Forked
perty, and lands which remain Dominion lands, on which entry is made until the patent is issued. The purpose of the committee was to remove the charge against such Dominion lands. The proposed section makes provision with regard to a settler who obtains Dominion lands, whether by soldier grant or otherwise, and thereafter secures the approval of the board to any advance to him pursuant to the act, "while there is owing by him to the board any sum or sums of money as the result of any sale made to him by the board or otherwise"; and we have to remember that a large part of the money advanced was advanced not for the purchase of land but for the purchase of stock and equipment, for improvement and other purposes. In many cases we found that the only land held by the man was that Dominion land together with stock and equipment; and we found it impossible to differentiate between the loan which would rightly apply to the one quarter-section alone, and loans applicable to the entire land at the time the loan was advanced. We therefore suggested that the land in possession of the settler at the time the money was advanced should be considered as security. In other words, that was the factor in the mind of the board at the time the money was loaned and was understood by the settler to be part of the security he had to offer. Under the former act, which we propose to repeal, that same man after receiving a loan made entry either by way of a soldier grant or on a homestead; and automatically that additional land was charged under the loan, although the land which he had just entered upon was not in the mind of the board at the time the loan was made, inasmuch as it was not in the possession of the settler when he received the advance. We found that the only practical method to adopt was to draw the dividing line afr the point when the loan was authorized. The land in the possession of the settler at that time would automatically come under the act, because we could not free it from the suggestion of being one of the factors that led to the loan. All land on which entry was made after the loan was advanced was free from that suggestion and would be free under the provisions of the act. The bill goes further than is apparent. After a man failed and the contract was rescinded and the land resold, the deficiency which remained was chargeable to the former settler as a debt which would automatically apply as a charge and a first mortgage against any land he might take up thereafter. Under this new section that land is free, because no soldier grant is subject to a charge of that kind.

When a settler obtains Dominion lands, whether by soldier grant or otherwise, and whether before or after having secured from the board any advance pursuant to this act, while there is owing by him to the board any sum or sums of money as a result of any sale made to him by the board, or otherwise by reason of the exercise by the board of any of its powers under this act, such sum so owing shall constitute a first charge on the lands so obtained and no patent shall be issued to such settler therefor until such sum or sums, with accrued interest, have been fully paid or repaid.
The whole thing is in the word "thereafter". After he has obtained what I call "new land", which might be Dominion land, or by soldier grant, or by homestead, he goes to the board and says, "I want a loan," whether it be for improvements or for stock, then everything he owned would be covered by that loan.

Would not the land be
specified? It is not specifying the land when he gets the loan that we object to.

I do not know anything
about the agreements, because I have never seen them.

If a loan is given to
anybody, the Soldier Settlement Board must necessarily specify the security upon which they give it.

At present it is not specified if I may call my hon. friend's attention to section 26-and every piece of land he obtains
is plastered by this mortgage to the land settlement board. It was the endeavour of the committee to make that clear, and the amendment was brought down. Whether we have succeeded in doing that or not, I do not know; I would not be quite sure myself. It was an honest endeavour on the part of the subcommittee to clean up that situation. Personally, I think it seems to cover the case. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), who has had far more experience that I have in dealing with land settlement, is also of the same opinion. My hon. friend from Melfort (Mr. McLean), who has a large number of soldier settlers in his constituency, seems to think that this fits the case. I have none in my constituency, and, for that reason perhaps I have not been so much interested in land settlement as I might be.

My hon. friend from
Red Deer made the statement a few minutes ago that the soldier who had obtained a loan upon his soldier land when he had a homestead, received that loan without anything being said in the agreement about the homestead. The hon. member said that the homestead having been a factor in securing that loan, it should be agreed upon that it was encumbered. That is the very point: that he gets a loan upon a quarter section, which is expressed in the agreement, and though the homestead that he had at the time he got the agreement was not referred to in the agreement, still it was encumbered. It is that very principle that we are discussing-that when a loan is granted the things secured by that loan should be specified in the agreement. The hon. member for Red Deer said that it was a factor in the board granting a loan, although they did not so specify it.

If no loan had been
made for the purchase of land the matter would' be very simple. The security would be specified and be limited to the land purchase. The difficulty is that many of the loans were not obtained for the purchase of lands, and so did not stipulate any particular class of land. They may have been for the purpose of purchasing stock, or for the purpose of placing permanent improvements on the land, such as buildings; or for the purpose of purchasing seed or feed, or sometimes subsidiary amounts in order to subsist. All of these loans were general loans; there was no specification made as to the land to which they applied, and in most of these cases, I venture to say, it is impossible to dissociate the Dominion land held by the settler at that time from the board land.

I should like to make this

Any future acquired property, whether it be stock or land, will be unencumbered and only the original land will be encumbered. The object of the committee surely is to free the future acquired property from the original mortgage. Therefore if we repeal section 26, we accomplish that purpose. The next thing is that we do not wish to prohibit that man from coming before the board again for a new loan. That is, I think, correct. If that man comes before the board and asks for a new loan, the board will say: What security have you? The man will say: Here is my homestead; here is my stock; here is some other subsequently acquired property; I will give you that. Why bother with this complicated section? Let us repeal the old section and thereby take the charge off the future acquired property. Then a man will have in his possession free all the property which he acquires after he put the mortgage on and he can offer that in the

future as security to the settlement board. I think that is the proper way of dealing with the present difficulty.

Might I suggest that the

The word "obtains" suggests something in the future and, the minister notwithstanding, this is intended to be retroactive to a large extent. When I say that a man obtains land, that refers to the future. This section is intended to cover also the past tense.

I understand that every settler has the right to take up a homestead without any question or discretion on the part of the Soldier Settlement Board or anyone else, but section 15 of the Soldier Settlement Act reads:

The point I want to raise is this: Will there be any trouble, so far as the soldier settler is concerned, in getting the right to take up a soldier grant provided that he has been salvaged and he still owes the board say $200 or $300? My hon. friend is referring

I can hardily answer that

speechtext: In my opinion the nays have it; I declare the motion lost. There is a motion that the name of the company be changed to the Central Finance Corporation.
The notice says "Federal Lending Company."

This legislation, I understand, is asked for in order to make it possible for corporations to lend money on second mortgages. Although ostensibly only 6 per cent is to be charged on money loaned, we are informed by the Superintendent of Insurance that, with the various charges, the rate will amount to about 18 or 20 per cent. I have no doubt that those who are promot-

ing the bill are perfectly right when they say that this will not be as high an interest as is charged by certain money lenders in such cities as Montreal. At the same time it is a usurious rate and it seems to me that something is wrong with our present financial institutions if it is necessary for us to get behind legislation like this, under which the borrower will ultimately have to pay about 18 per cent. The only ground on which one could possibly support this bill is that under it the evil will not be as great as that which prevails at the present time with money lenders who charge much higher rates. As regards the name, I do not think that the word "Finance" should be used. When we use that word we associate it with the highest type of financial institutions in the country. The name does not seem to me to be a proper one to designate a money lending institution whose various charges will eventually run up to as high as 18 per cent.

I wish to protest against this bill. Some of us can remember the ruin caused by the York County Loan Company, and the suffering entailed in Parkdale, West York and other places. I protest against parliament granting a charter to the persons named in this bill-Lawrence Kert, David Sher and two or three stenographers. How do we know who the company are? Do we know anything of its bona fides? What are its powers? It will lend money on second mortgages at any rate it likes to poor people. I submit that the powers of this company are beyond the scope of this parliament. The company will deal in chattel mortgages, lien notes, second mortgages and all that kind of thing and its purposes will be purely provincial and local in Toronto. This company is to have its head office in the city of Toronto, but we have had enough companies there incorporated by this parliament, such as the Farmers' Bank, the Home Bank, the Sovereign Bank, the York Loan Company and many others, all of which have failed and caused great ruin and loss to thousands. You will notice what these gentlemen propose to do; they desire to suspend three federal acts, the Money Lenders Act, the Interest Act and the Loan Companies Act, all of which have been passed for the protection of the working classes in our large cities. No one knows what interest this company will charge on these second mortgages; this parliament is asked to release the company from the control of these acts. A

Federal Loan Company
similar bill came up in this house two or three years ago, and I took the ground then that we did not have sufficient protection for our people and that this parliament had no jurisdiction. On general principles I protest against incorporating companies such as this, which give no security or protection to the public from extortionate rates of interest.

poor people of Toronto from the failure of similar companies, such as the Home Bank, the Farmers' Bank and the York Loan Company, and so long as I am a member of this house I will protest against the incorporating here of purely provincial companies of this kind, which attempt to secure a charter from this parliament by some change of name or some play on words so as to escape provincial supervision. If this sort of thing is to go on the sooner the Minister of Finance brings in a new Loan Companies Act the better it will be, if the public are to be protected from extortionate rates. As a lawyer I have seen something of the suffering caused among the poor people of Toronto, by the failure of some of these loan companies of this kind, and I wish to protest against interference by this parliament with the government of Ontario in its control of purely provincial companies of this kind, which are not by the widest stretch of the imagination proper companies to give a charter to here.
